title: Essential Oils: Nature's Cure?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain essential oils: volatile organic compounds stored in plant glands that give plants their scent, and why the term 'essential oil' traces to alchemists and Paracelsus's 'quintessence.' They cover the history from ancient Egypt through the Persians, Middle Ages, and Paracelsus; extraction methods (enfleurage, maceration, cold expression, steam distillation, ultrasound-assisted extraction) and why oils are expensive (e.g., five metric tons of rose petals per kilogram). They discuss the small number of studies on antimicrobial, antifungal, and neurochemical effects (lavender and serotonin transporters), the lack of FDA regulation, multi-level marketing sellers making unfounded health and pregnancy claims, and the danger of claiming oils cure serious diseases like Ebola. The episode opens with a long book pre-order plug and includes a sponsor-style plug for Emily's small business, and ends with listener mail about bruxism and jaw surgery.
topics: Stuff You Should Know book preorder

segments.title: Book pre-order plug and intro
segments.summary: Hosts promote their upcoming book and pre-order poster gift, then open the show.

segments.title: Intro to essential oils
segments.summary: Hosts introduce essential oils as plant compounds used for communication, noting scent functions in plants and animals and that many plant parts hold oils.

segments.title: Chemistry of essential oils
segments.summary: Essential oils are divided into oxygenated compounds and hydrocarbons (terpenes); they are volatile organic compounds that evaporate at low temperatures. Peppermint's menthol is one component among many that make up the oil's full scent.

segments.title: Origin of the term essential oil
segments.summary: The term comes from alchemists and Paracelsus's idea of a fifth element, quinta essentia, shortened to essential oil.

segments.title: History from ancient Egypt to the Middle Ages
segments.summary: Essential oils were used in ancient Egypt, traditional Chinese medicine, and by the Greeks, Romans and Persians; Persians distilled ethyl alcohol from sugar, which aided extraction; the practice reached Europe in the Middle Ages. Paracelsus pushed for evidence-based science.

segments.title: Why essential oils are expensive and extraction methods
segments.summary: Oils require large amounts of plant material (about five metric tons of rose petals per kilogram of rose oil). Methods discussed include enfleurage (fat absorption), maceration (warm fat version, and a separate culinary sense), and cold expression of citrus peels.

segments.title: Steam distillation and ultrasound extraction
segments.summary: Steam distillation passes steam through plant material, condensing into oil and water that separate. Ultrasound can break cell walls to extract more oil at lower temperatures and with less plant material.

segments.title: Uses and antimicrobial research
segments.summary: Essential oils are used as preservatives, flavorings, scents, insect repellents, and agricultural agents. Studies show some oils such as clove and tea tree are antimicrobial or antifungal, and research explores them as alternatives to drug-resistant pathogens like MRSA.

segments.title: Aromatherapy and the lavender serotonin study
segments.summary: Aromatherapy works by inhaling volatile compounds that stimulate the olfactory system. Lavender compound linalool has been studied for effects on serotonin transporters and NMDA receptors, but hosts stress this does not make lavender a cure for depression.

segments.title: Marketing claims, FDA regulation, and dangerous claims
segments.summary: Essential oils fall in a gray area between drugs and cosmetics and are not FDA-approved for health claims. Multi-level marketing sellers make unfounded claims, including about pregnancy and curing serious diseases like Ebola, and some oils such as rosemary may be harmful during pregnancy.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener Erica writes about bruxism and jaw surgery; hosts sign off.
